newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Yeltsin priority to reassert Kremlin control.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Yeltsin priority to reassert Kremlin control.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's political priority after his heart operation is to reassert control over the Kremlin and restore the balance of power upset by months of infighting.

If his health allows him to do this, Yeltsin is then likely to try to shift the focus away from the power struggles and back to tackling the economic and political problems that have piled up in his absence from the Kremlin.
His long-term goal, political analysts say, would be to groom a successor for a presidential election which looks ncreasingly likely to go ahead as planned in the year 2000 and not sooner.

"The first thing he will want to do after he has recovered is to show he is in complete control. This is vital in a system where the president has huge powers," said Irina Kobrinskaya, an analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Doctors still say it is not clear how full a recovery the 65-year-old president will make, although they say he could be back at his Kremlin desk in six to eight weeks.
Even before Yeltsin resumes normal work, he is sure to be considering ways to ensure no single group has the upper hand in the corridors of power.
This may mean checking the rise of Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, a clear winner in the battle for influence which intensfied in Yeltsin's absence as he prepared for his bypass operation.

Many politicians say the 41-year-old former privatisation guru plotted the downfall of national security adviser Alexander Lebed, who was sacked by Yeltsin on October 17 for having open presidential ambitions.
"Yeltsin likes to balance one force off against another. He will want to make sure no single person or group is dominant and that could mean cutting Chubais down to size," Kobrinskaya said.
Although Yeltsin appears unlikely to sack Chubais, who masterminded his reelection on July 3, he may look for other ways to show he is the boss.
One way would be to dismiss Boris Berezovsky, a Chubais ally appointed to the influential Security Council last week despite a lack of expertise in security matters.

The opposition communists said the appointment showed that Chubais had usurped his powers and their representative pulled out of a new four-man consultative council intended by Yeltsin to draw the communists into debate on some policy issues.

"One of the groups in the Kremlin has got too much influence and a good way for Yeltsin to show who is the master of the house would be to reprimand Chubais," said Andrei Piontkowski of the Centre for Strategic Studies thinktank.
"He could repay Chubais by firing Berezovsky," he said.

Yeltsin will not be content unless he makes a complete recovery which, in political terms, would enable him to take the Kremlin off auto-pilot and discourage any hopes Lebed or the communists might have of an early presidential election.

"He wants to stop the presidential race in its tracks. It looks obvious now that the presidential election will be in the year 2000 and this will give him a chance to groom his successor," Piontkowski said.
Many politicians see Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, a loyal ally, as the natural successor to Yeltsin -- barred under the constitution from seeking a third term.
But Yeltsin could plump for Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov or another candidate if the stolid premier fails to improve his dour public image in the next two or three years.

Yeltsin's hopes of keeping control and assuring stability will be challenged by deep economic problems, demonstrated in protests in several major cities on Tuesday by workers demanding the wages they have not been paid for several months.
The government has promised to pay those wages -- a move which would increase the strain in other areas of the economy.

Other problems are finding a political solution to the crisis in breakaway Chechnya and difficulties caused by a series of local elections in the next few weeks which look set to reduce the regions' dependence on the Kremlin.

"The president must tackle the current problems such as personnel and the presidential structures, but then he has to think about the problems ahead," said Viktor Borisyuk, until recently deputy head of the president's analytical centre.
"Top of the list of problems are wages, the regions and Chechnya. Letting social problems continue to pile up would be a very dangerous policy."
